The left bar stacks the three shares into the total gap (share $=1$; total log gap $D_{\text{total}}=1.035$, 95\% CI $[0.957, 1.108]$). The other three bars show each channel's share of the gap with 95\% percentile confidence intervals from 2{,}000 concept bootstraps, with terciles and volume quintiles recomputed in each resample. The sample is the held-out pool (PHYS, LIFEENV, SOC, MATHDEC), volume-stratified, excluding Medicine homes ($n=1{,}825$ concepts). Early contact accounts for 73\% of the gap (0.733, $[0.688, 0.789]$), retention for 25\% (0.254, $[0.213, 0.298]$), and frontier advance for close to zero (0.013, $[-0.027, 0.047]$). The shares are an accounting identity for the breadth outcome, not causal effects.}
  \label{fig:decomposition}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Diffusion trajectories: a continuum, not types}

We tested whether concepts cluster into discrete trajectory types (localised
emergence, rapid interdisciplinary diffusion, gradual integration) using DTW
$k$-medoids and HMM-based clustering on state sequences of field presence. No
trajectory typology passes a naming rule: the adjusted Rand index between DTW
$k = 4$ and HMM $S = 5$ is 0.222, and held-out re-clustering gives ARI $= 0.44$.
Instead, PCA reveals a continuum: PC1 (38.8\% of variance) is a
breadth-of-spread axis, and PC2 (10.7\%) is a keep-versus-lose axis. Early
openness (OPEN) correlates with PC1 beyond B5 (held-out DerSimonian--Laird
partial correlation 0.120, $I^2 = 0$) but not with PC2.

\subsection{Replication on vocabulary-free concepts}

To test whether the openness signal depends on the legacy concept lexicon, we
constructed a separate frame of 636 newborn title noun phrases (onsets
2003--2015) absent from the 56,643 legacy concepts. On this frame,
OPEN\textsubscript{home} shows a partial Spearman with rarefied breadth
($O_{2r}$, $m = 30$) of $+0.117$ [$+0.020$, $+0.218$] at the third control
rung, and neighbourhood novelty and churn of $+0.108$ [$+0.007$, $+0.211$].
Three of four estimable domain groups are positive. The verdict is partial: the
confidence interval on OPEN\textsubscript{home} includes zero at R5, and the
Holm-corrected $p$-value is 0.052.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

Our results address both research questions posed in the Introduction.

For RQ1, seven temporal network indicators predict cross-field breadth beyond a
strong popularity baseline, and these indicators generalise across four held-out
scientific domain groups. The strongest are contact reach (the count of off-home
fields already entered) and neighbourhood novelty (the share of new
co-occurrence partners). A learned model improves Spearman correlation by
$+0.059$ over the baseline. The practical forecasting gain is modest: B5 already
explains most of the variance, and OPEN adds only $+0.002$ Spearman on the
fresh cohort. The signal identifies which concepts are structurally positioned
for broader diffusion, rather than providing strong individual-level forecasts.

The confound analysis reveals that the signal is topical non-redundancy, a
static structural property of the home topic mix, rather than temporal partner
turnover. A concept whose early partners span multiple communities and introduce
novel topical connections tends to spread more broadly, but this tendency is set
by the concept's position in the knowledge network rather than by dynamic churn.

For RQ2, the retained-frontier model confirms that concepts spread next to
fields related to the ones currently retaining them. This extends the principle
of relatedness from economic geography \citep{Hidalgo2007, Neffke2011}, where
regions diversify into products related to their existing portfolio, to
scientific concept diffusion. The novel element is retention: it is not merely
which fields have adopted a concept that predicts the next field, but which of
those fields continue to use it. The volume-matched contrast is null, however,
indicating that retention and volume are confounded and that the pure retention
signal cannot be isolated at this sample size.

The breadth decomposition shows that the gap between integrating and localised
concepts is set early by contact diversity (73\%) rather than by continued
frontier advance (1\%). This echoes \citet{Weng2013}, who found that early
community diversity predicts virality, and extends it from social media to
scientific knowledge networks.

The reconciliation with \citet{Cheng2023} reveals an outcome-dependent split:
consistency predicts volume growth (size-dominated) but narrower cross-field
reach. The two findings are compatible because volume growth and cross-field
breadth are partially independent outcomes.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

Several limitations bound the scope of these results.

First, concept identification relies on title matching against a legacy lexicon
that over-represents the natural sciences and computer science. The
vocabulary-free replication partially addresses this, but its sample is smaller
and the verdict is partial.

Second, the field backbone uses a fixed 26-field classification from OpenAlex.
A finer-grained classification would produce more adoption episodes but also
more noise in field assignment. Our results are conditioned on this specific
resolution.

Third, the retained-frontier claim is partial by its own pre-registered rule:
the volume-matched contrast is null, meaning that we cannot distinguish the
effect of retention from that of volume. A larger sample with more fine-grained
volume controls would be needed to isolate pure retention.

Fourth, the openness signal's practical forecasting value is small ($+0.002$
Spearman on the fresh cohort). The indicators characterise rather than predict:
they identify structural preconditions for broad diffusion but do not yield
individually actionable forecasts.

Fifth, outcomes are measured at $t_0 + 6$ to $t_0 + 8$, a horizon of 6--8
years after concept onset. Longer horizons might reveal different dynamics, and
our results do not speak to very long-term disciplinary integration.

Sixth, the analysis is observational. Early network structure is correlated with
later breadth, but we cannot establish that it causes broader diffusion. The
within-concept panel analysis suggests that the association is a
between-concept trait rather than a within-concept mechanism.

Seventh, the held-out outcomes were previously unsealed by two earlier
experiments in the same project, so the indicator-screen held-out results are
robustness checks within the same frame rather than fully independent
confirmations. The fresh 2015--2017 cohort is the only body never used in any
prior step.

Eighth, Mathematics and Decision Sciences is underpowered in both the indicator
screen (165 concepts) and the retained-frontier model ($d_0 = 0.065$, CI
includes zero), so our results may not generalise to this domain.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We have shown that early structural signals in a concept's co-occurrence network
predict later cross-field breadth across multiple scientific domains, that
concepts spread next to fields related to the ones currently retaining them, and
that early contact diversity, not continued frontier advance, accounts for most
of the breadth difference between integrating and localised concepts. The
openness signal is topical non-redundancy of the home neighbourhood, not
temporal partner turnover. These findings connect the literatures on concept
diffusion in science \citep{Cheng2023}, the principle of relatedness from
economic geography \citep{Hidalgo2007}, and community structure in social
contagion \citep{Weng2013, Ugander2012}, offering a network-level account of
why some scientific concepts become broadly integrated while others remain local.

Under a minimum-conditional-probability\nproximity \\citep{Hidalgo2007}, the retained-frontier coefficient reverses to\n$-0.021$ ($p = 0.012$), indicating backbone dependence.\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Retained-frontier coefficient $d_0$ from the conditional-logit model\nof next-field entry across domain groups and the 2010--2014 cohort, with 95\\%\nconcept-clustered confidence intervals.}\n\\label{tab:retained_frontier}\n\\begin{tabular}{l c c c}\n\\toprule\nModel & $d_0$ coefficient & 95\\% CI (concept) & Likelihood ratio \\\\\n\\midrule\nDevelopment set & 0.228 & $[0.164, 0.291]$ & 34.5 \\\\\nHeld-out pooled & 0.322 & $[0.291, 0.355]$ & 325.8 \\\\\nPhysical Sciences & 0.148 & $[0.078, 0.219]$ & -- \\\\\nLife \\& Environment & 0.401 & $[0.342, 0.460]$ & -- \\\\\nSocial Sciences & 0.297 & $[0.246, 0.348]$ & -- \\\\\nMath \\& Decision Sci. & 0.065 & $[-0.109, 0.239]$ & -- \\\\\n2010--2014 cohort & 0.321 & $[0.292, 0.347]$ & -- \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig3_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Retained-frontier coefficient $d_0$ from the conditional-logit model of next-field entry, estimated on held-out data. $d_0$ measures how much a target field's relatedness to the fields currently retaining a concept predicts entry into it. It is net of relatedness to the home field, field size, entered-field density and gateway centrality, and is expressed in log-odds per standard deviation. Blue circles are the estimates for the four held-out domain groups (top) and for the 2010--14 held-out cohort. Horizontal bars are 95\\% Wald confidence intervals from concept-clustered standard errors, and $n$ is the number of entry events. The dark diamond spans the DerSimonian--Laird random-effects pooled estimate over the four groups, 0.243 [0.118, 0.368], with $I^2 = 0.92$. The dashed vertical line marks $d_0 = 0$, and the right-hand column prints each estimate with its interval. The point estimate is positive in all four groups and in the cohort. The interval excludes zero for Physical Sciences, Life \\& Env., Social Sciences and the cohort. Math \\& Decision ($n = 296$) is the weak, imprecise group, 0.065 [$-0.109$, 0.239], and together with Life \\& Env.\\ (0.401) it drives the high heterogeneity. These are associations. In the same experiment, a volume-matched contrast between retaining and non-retaining fields is null ($-0.028$ [$-0.105$, 0.046]; not plotted), so the pre-registered frontier test is only partially supported: persistence is confounded with volume.}\n  \\label{fig:retained_frontier}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig4_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Nested conditional-logit models of field entry on the held-out frame (3,162 concepts, 6,978 entry events, 6,076 informative concept-year strata). R0: home relatedness + log field size + entered-field density + own-field gateway centrality; R1: + RCA-based density; R2: + volume-weighted density; R3: + retained-frontier relatedness. (a)~Within-stratum AUC of each rung. Blue circles, solid line: primary specification using backbone relatedness. Amber squares, dashed line: sensitivity rebuild using minimum conditional-probability proximity. (b)~Likelihood-ratio $\\chi^2$ (df $=1$, log scale) for the term each rung adds over the previous rung. Solid blue bars: primary. Hatched amber bars: sensitivity. The dotted line marks $p=0.05$ ($\\chi^2=3.84$). In the primary specification, the retained-frontier term gives the largest step (LR $=325.8$, $p<10^{-72}$), but AUC rises only from 0.847 to 0.852. The volume-density step is not significant (LR $=1.9$). Under minimum conditional-probability proximity, baseline discrimination is higher and the retained-frontier term adds no AUC (0.867 to 0.866; LR $=6.3$). The increment therefore depends on the proximity definition. No confidence intervals on AUC are available.}\n  \\label{fig:model_ladder}\n\\end{figure}\n\nThe within-stratum AUC increases from 0.847 (R2: baseline + RCA density +\nvolume density) to 0.852 (R3: + retained-frontier relatedness). The increment\nis small because field size alone achieves AUC 0.76, density only 0.59, and the\nceiling is constrained by having only 26 fields.\n\n\\subsubsection{Gateway centrality does not predict retention}\n\nA separate pre-registered test asks whether the adopting field's eigenvector\ncentrality on the backbone predicts retention. On 27,393 held-out episodes, the\ngateway-centrality increment is effectively zero: $\\Delta$-AUC $-0.00001$\n[$-0.0006$, $+0.0003$]. The minimum detectable effect is 0.004. Gateway alone\nhas AUC 0.605 on DEV versus 0.506 on held-out: the DEV signal is\ndomain-specific. Verdict: disconfirmed.\n\n\\subsubsection{Breadth decomposition}\n\nWe decompose the gap in retained off-home breadth between the top and bottom\n$O_{2r}$ terciles into log $E_2$ (early contact), log $M$ (frontier advance)\nand log $\\rho$ (retention). Volume-stratified, on the held-out pool excluding\nMedicine (to avoid a domain that dominates the localised class):\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n  \\item Early contact share: 73.3\\%\n  \\item Frontier advance share: 1.3\\%\n  \\item Retention share: 25.4\\%\n  \\item Difference (exploration minus retention): 0.492 [$0.403$, $0.575$]\n\\end{itemize}\n\nThe DerSimonian--Laird pool of the exploration-retention difference across three\nheld-out groups is 0.504 [$0.329$, $0.679$] with $I^2 = 0.76$.\n\nBreadth differences between concepts are set by how many fields a concept\ncontacts early, not by how many more it enters later. Frontier advance, the\nratio of fields at $t_0 + 8$ to those at $t_0 + 2$, contributes near zero\nbecause both broad and narrow concepts gain new fields at similar rates relative\nto their base.\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig5_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Decomposition of the gap in retained off-home breadth (log scale) between the top and bottom $O_{2r}$ tercile into three multiplicative channels: early contact ($E_2$, green), frontier advance ($M$, light grey) and retention ($\\rho$, blue). The left bar stacks the three shares into the total gap (share $=1$; total log gap $D_{\\text{total}}=1.035$, 95\\% CI $[0.957, 1.108]$). The other three bars show each channel's share of the gap with 95\\% percentile confidence intervals from 2{,}000 concept bootstraps, with terciles and volume quintiles recomputed in each resample. The sample is the held-out pool (PHYS, LIFEENV, SOC, MATHDEC), volume-stratified, excluding Medicine homes ($n=1{,}825$ concepts). Early contact accounts for 73\\% of the gap (0.733, $[0.688, 0.789]$), retention for 25\\% (0.254, $[0.213, 0.298]$), and frontier advance for close to zero (0.013, $[-0.027, 0.047]$). The shares are an accounting identity for the breadth outcome, not causal effects.}\n  \\label{fig:decomposition}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsubsection{Diffusion trajectories: a continuum, not types}\n\nWe tested whether concepts cluster into discrete trajectory types (localised\nemergence, rapid interdisciplinary diffusion, gradual integration) using DTW\n$k$-medoids and HMM-based clustering on state sequences of field presence. No\ntrajectory typology passes a naming rule: the adjusted Rand index between DTW\n$k = 4$ and HMM $S = 5$ is 0.222, and held-out re-clustering gives ARI $= 0.44$.\nInstead, PCA reveals a continuum: PC1 (38.8\\% of variance) is a\nbreadth-of-spread axis, and PC2 (10.7\\%) is a keep-versus-lose axis. Early\nopenness (OPEN) correlates with PC1 beyond B5 (held-out DerSimonian--Laird\npartial correlation 0.120, $I^2 = 0$) but not with PC2.\n\n\\subsection{Replication on vocabulary-free concepts}\n\nTo test whether the openness signal depends on the legacy concept lexicon, we\nconstructed a separate frame of 636 newborn title noun phrases (onsets\n2003--2015) absent from the 56,643 legacy concepts. On this frame,\nOPEN\\textsubscript{home} shows a partial Spearman with rarefied breadth\n($O_{2r}$, $m = 30$) of $+0.117$ [$+0.020$, $+0.218$] at the third control\nrung, and neighbourhood novelty and churn of $+0.108$ [$+0.007$, $+0.211$].\nThree of four estimable domain groups are positive. The verdict is partial: the\nconfidence interval on OPEN\\textsubscript{home} includes zero at R5, and the\nHolm-corrected $p$-value is 0.052.\n\n%% ===================================================================\n\\section{Discussion}\n\\label{sec:discussion}\n\nOur results address both research questions posed in the Introduction.\n\nFor RQ1, seven temporal network indicators predict cross-field breadth beyond a\nstrong popularity baseline, and these indicators generalise across four held-out\nscientific domain groups. The strongest are contact reach (the count of off-home\nfields already entered) and neighbourhood novelty (the share of new\nco-occurrence partners). A learned model improves Spearman correlation by\n$+0.059$ over the baseline. The practical forecasting gain is modest: B5 already\nexplains most of the variance, and OPEN adds only $+0.002$ Spearman on the\nfresh cohort. The signal identifies which concepts are structurally positioned\nfor broader diffusion, rather than providing strong individual-level forecasts.\n\nThe confound analysis reveals that the signal is topical non-redundancy, a\nstatic structural property of the home topic mix, rather than temporal partner\nturnover. A concept whose early partners span multiple communities and introduce\nnovel topical connections tends to spread more broadly, but this tendency is set\nby the concept's position in the knowledge network rather than by dynamic churn.\n\nFor RQ2, the retained-frontier model confirms that concepts spread next to\nfields related to the ones currently retaining them. This extends the principle\nof relatedness from economic geography \\citep{Hidalgo2007, Neffke2011}, where\nregions diversify into products related to their existing portfolio, to\nscientific concept diffusion. The novel element is retention: it is not merely\nwhich fields have adopted a concept that predicts the next field, but which of\nthose fields continue to use it. The volume-matched contrast is null, however,\nindicating that retention and volume are confounded and that the pure retention\nsignal cannot be isolated at this sample size.\n\nThe breadth decomposition shows that the gap between integrating and localised\nconcepts is set early by contact diversity (73\\%) rather than by continued\nfrontier advance (1\\%). This echoes \\citet{Weng2013}, who found that early\ncommunity diversity predicts virality, and extends it from social media to\nscientific knowledge networks.\n\nThe reconciliation with \\citet{Cheng2023} reveals an outcome-dependent split:\nconsistency predicts volume growth (size-dominated) but narrower cross-field\nreach. The two findings are compatible because volume growth and cross-field\nbreadth are partially independent outcomes.\n\n%% ===================================================================\n\\section{Limitations}\n\\label{sec:limitations}\n\nSeveral limitations bound the scope of these results.\n\nFirst, concept identification relies on title matching against a legacy lexicon\nthat over-represents the natural sciences and computer science. The\nvocabulary-free replication partially addresses this, but its sample is smaller\nand the verdict is partial.\n\nSecond, the field backbone uses a fixed 26-field classification from OpenAlex.\nA finer-grained classification would produce more adoption episodes but also\nmore noise in field assignment. Our results are conditioned on this specific\nresolution.\n\nThird, the retained-frontier claim is partial by its own pre-registered rule:\nthe volume-matched contrast is null, meaning that we cannot distinguish the\neffect of retention from that of volume. A larger sample with more fine-grained\nvolume controls would be needed to isolate pure retention.\n\nFourth, the openness signal's practical forecasting value is small ($+0.002$\nSpearman on the fresh cohort). The indicators characterise rather than predict:\nthey identify structural preconditions for broad diffusion but do not yield\nindividually actionable forecasts.\n\nFifth, outcomes are measured at $t_0 + 6$ to $t_0 + 8$, a horizon of 6--8\nyears after concept onset. Longer horizons might reveal different dynamics, and\nour results do not speak to very long-term disciplinary integration.\n\nSixth, the analysis is observational. Early network structure is correlated with\nlater breadth, but we cannot establish that it causes broader diffusion. The\nwithin-concept panel analysis suggests that the association is a\nbetween-concept trait rather than a within-concept mechanism.\n\nSeventh, the held-out outcomes were previously unsealed by two earlier\nexperiments in the same project, so the indicator-screen held-out results are\nrobustness checks within the same frame rather than fully independent\nconfirmations. The fresh 2015--2017 cohort is the only body never used in any\nprior step.\n\nEighth, Mathematics and Decision Sciences is underpowered in both the indicator\nscreen (165 concepts) and the retained-frontier model ($d_0 = 0.065$, CI\nincludes zero), so our results may not generalise to this domain.\n\n%% ===================================================================\n\\section{Conclusion}\n\\label{sec:conclusion}\n\nWe have shown that early structural signals in a concept's co-occurrence network\npredict later cross-field breadth across multiple scientific domains, that\nconcepts spread next to fields related to the ones currently retaining them, and\nthat early contact diversity, not continued frontier advance, accounts for most\nof the breadth difference between integrating and localised concepts. The\nopenness signal is topical non-redundancy of the home neighbourhood, not\ntemporal partner turnover. These findings connect the literatures on concept\ndiffusion in science \\citep{Cheng2023}, the principle of relatedness from\neconomic geography \\citep{Hidalgo2007}, and community structure in social\ncontagion \\citep{Weng2013, Ugander2012}, offering a network-level account of\nwhy some scientific concepts become broadly integrated while others remain local.\n\n%% ===================================================================\n\\bibliographystyle{plainnat}\n\\bibliography{references}\n\n\\end{document}\n", "structuredPatch": [], "originalFile": null, "userModified": false}

Any network indicator must add\ninformation beyond these baselines. Entry is defined as the concept reaching 5 grounded\npublications in the field. For\ncitation growth, home-field relatedness (negative) and author growth are\nconfirmed but the learned model reaches only Spearman 0.188 against B5's 0.015.\nExternal recognition shows no association with any network indicator beyond\nonset year.\n\n\\subsection{Openness composite and confirmation}\n\nThe six ego-network components of the confirmed indicators compose into an\nopenness index (OPEN), defined as the mean of six $z$-scored components with\nconstants frozen on the full 12,499-concept frame.\n\nOn a fresh 2015--2017 onset cohort of 1,443 concepts never used in any selection\nstep, OPEN measured within the home field (OPEN\\textsubscript{home}) shows a\npartial Spearman correlation with $O_{2r}$ of $+0.091$ [$+0.013$, $+0.171$] at\nthe second control rung (controlling for B5, onset year and contact reach), and\n$+0.080$ [$+0.001$, $+0.162$] at the third rung (adding concept type and\npre-onset footprint). The\nsignal carries no forecasting gain over B5 ($+0.002$ Spearman). In the same experiment, a volume-matched contrast between retaining and non-retaining fields is null ($-0.028$ [$-0.105$, 0.046]; not plotted), so the pre-registered frontier test is only partially supported: persistence is confounded with volume.}\n  \\label{fig:retained_frontier}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig4_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Nested conditional-logit models of field entry on the held-out frame (3,162 concepts, 6,978 entry events, 6,076 informative concept-year strata). R0: home relatedness + log field size + entered-field density + own-field gateway centrality; R1: + RCA-based density; R2: + volume-weighted density; R3: + retained-frontier relatedness. (a)~Within-stratum AUC of each rung. Blue circles, solid line: primary specification using backbone relatedness. Amber squares, dashed line: sensitivity rebuild using minimum conditional-probability proximity. (b)~Likelihood-ratio $\\chi^2$ (df $=1$, log scale) for the term each rung adds over the previous rung. Solid blue bars: primary. Hatched amber bars: sensitivity. The dotted line marks $p=0.05$ ($\\chi^2=3.84$). In the primary specification, the retained-frontier term gives the largest step (LR $=325.8$, $p<10^{-72}$), but AUC rises only from 0.847 to 0.852. The volume-density step is not significant (LR $=1.9$). Under minimum conditional-probability proximity, baseline discrimination is higher and the retained-frontier term adds no AUC (0.867 to 0.866; LR $=6.3$). The increment therefore depends on the proximity definition. No confidence intervals on AUC are available.}\n  \\label{fig:model_ladder}\n\\end{figure}\n\nThe within-stratum AUC increases from 0.847 (R2: baseline + RCA density +\nvolume density) to 0.852 (R3: + retained-frontier relatedness). The increment\nis small because field size alone achieves AUC 0.76, density only 0.59, and the\nceiling is constrained by having only 26 fields.\n\n\\subsubsection{Gateway centrality does not predict retention}\n\nA separate pre-registered test asks whether the adopting field's eigenvector\ncentrality on the backbone predicts retention. On 27,393 held-out episodes, the\ngateway-centrality increment is effectively zero: $\\Delta$-AUC $-0.00001$\n[$-0.0006$, $+0.0003$]. The minimum detectable effect is 0.004. Gateway alone\nhas AUC 0.605 on DEV versus 0.506 on held-out: the DEV signal is\ndomain-specific. Verdict: disconfirmed.\n\n\\subsubsection{Breadth decomposition}\n\nWe decompose the gap in retained off-home breadth between the top and bottom\n$O_{2r}$ terciles into log $E_2$ (early contact), log $M$ (frontier advance)\nand log $\\rho$ (retention). Volume-stratified, on the held-out pool excluding\nMedicine (to avoid a domain that dominates the localised class):\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n  \\item Early contact share: 73.3\\%\n  \\item Frontier advance share: 1.3\\%\n  \\item Retention share: 25.4\\%\n  \\item Difference (exploration minus retention): 0.492 [$0.403$, $0.575$]\n\\end{itemize}\n\nThe DerSimonian--Laird pool of the exploration-retention difference across three\nheld-out groups is 0.504 [$0.329$, $0.679$] with $I^2 = 0.76$.\n\nBreadth differences between concepts are set by how many fields a concept\ncontacts early, not by how many more it enters later. Frontier advance, the\nratio of fields at $t_0 + 8$ to those at $t_0 + 2$, contributes near zero\nbecause both broad and narrow concepts gain new fields at similar rates relative\nto their base.\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig5_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Decomposition of the gap in retained off-home breadth (log scale) between the top and bottom $O_{2r}$ tercile into three multiplicative channels: early contact ($E_2$, green), frontier advance ($M$, light grey) and retention ($\\rho$, blue). The left bar stacks the three shares into the total gap (share $=1$; total log gap $D_{\\text{total}}=1.035$, 95\\% CI $[0.957, 1.108]$). The other three bars show each channel's share of the gap with 95\\% percentile confidence intervals from 2{,}000 concept bootstraps, with terciles and volume quintiles recomputed in each resample. The sample is the held-out pool (PHYS, LIFEENV, SOC, MATHDEC), volume-stratified, excluding Medicine homes ($n=1{,}825$ concepts). Early contact accounts for 73\\% of the gap (0.733, $[0.688, 0.789]$), retention for 25\\% (0.254, $[0.213, 0.298]$), and frontier advance for close to zero (0.013, $[-0.027, 0.047]$). The shares are an accounting identity for the breadth outcome, not causal effects.}\n  \\label{fig:decomposition}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsubsection{Diffusion trajectories: a continuum, not types}\n\nWe tested whether concepts cluster into discrete trajectory types (localised\nemergence, rapid interdisciplinary diffusion, gradual integration) using DTW\n$k$-medoids and HMM-based clustering on state sequences of field presence. No\ntrajectory typology passes a naming rule: the adjusted Rand index between DTW\n$k = 4$ and HMM $S = 5$ is 0.222, and held-out re-clustering gives ARI $= 0.44$.\nInstead, PCA reveals a continuum: PC1 (38.8\\% of variance) is a\nbreadth-of-spread axis, and PC2 (10.7\\%) is a keep-versus-lose axis. Early\nopenness (OPEN) correlates with PC1 beyond B5 (held-out DerSimonian--Laird\npartial correlation 0.120, $I^2 = 0$) but not with PC2.\n\n\\subsection{Replication on vocabulary-free concepts}\n\nTo test whether the openness signal depends on the legacy concept lexicon, we\nconstructed a separate frame of 636 newborn title noun phrases (onsets\n2003--2015) absent from the 56,643 legacy concepts. On this frame,\nOPEN\\textsubscript{home} shows a partial Spearman with rarefied breadth\n($O_{2r}$, $m = 30$) of $+0.117$ [$+0.020$, $+0.218$] at the third control\nrung, and neighbourhood novelty and churn of $+0.108$ [$+0.007$, $+0.211$].\nThree of four estimable domain groups are positive. The verdict is partial: the\nconfidence interval on OPEN\\textsubscript{home} includes zero at R5, and the\nHolm-corrected $p$-value is 0.052.\n\n%% ===================================================================\n\\section{Discussion}\n\\label{sec:discussion}\n\nOur results address both research questions posed in the Introduction.\n\nFor RQ1, seven temporal network indicators predict cross-field breadth beyond a\nstrong popularity baseline, and these indicators generalise across four held-out\nscientific domain groups. The strongest are contact reach (the count of off-home\nfields already entered) and neighbourhood novelty (the share of new\nco-occurrence partners). A learned model improves Spearman correlation by\n$+0.059$ over the baseline. The practical forecasting gain is modest: B5 already\nexplains most of the variance, and OPEN adds only $+0.002$ Spearman on the\nfresh cohort. The signal identifies which concepts are structurally positioned\nfor broader diffusion, rather than providing strong individual-level forecasts.\n\nThe confound analysis reveals that the signal is topical non-redundancy, a\nstatic structural property of the home topic mix, rather than temporal partner\nturnover. A concept whose early partners span multiple communities and introduce\nnovel topical connections tends to spread more broadly, but this tendency is set\nby the concept's position in the knowledge network rather than by dynamic churn.\n\nFor RQ2, the retained-frontier model confirms that concepts spread next to\nfields related to the ones currently retaining them. This extends the principle\nof relatedness from economic geography \\citep{Hidalgo2007, Neffke2011}, where\nregions diversify into products related to their existing portfolio, to\nscientific concept diffusion. The novel element is retention: it is not merely\nwhich fields have adopted a concept that predicts the next field, but which of\nthose fields continue to use it. The volume-matched contrast is null, however,\nindicating that retention and volume are confounded and that the pure retention\nsignal cannot be isolated at this sample size.\n\nThe breadth decomposition shows that the gap between integrating and localised\nconcepts is set early by contact diversity (73\\%) rather than by continued\nfrontier advance (1\\%). This echoes \\citet{Weng2013}, who found that early\ncommunity diversity predicts virality, and extends it from social media to\nscientific knowledge networks.\n\nThe reconciliation with \\citet{Cheng2023} reveals an outcome-dependent split:\nconsistency predicts volume growth (size-dominated) but narrower cross-field\nreach. The two findings are compatible because volume growth and cross-field\nbreadth are partially independent outcomes.\n\n%% ===================================================================\n\\section{Limitations}\n\\label{sec:limitations}\n\nSeveral limitations bound the scope of these results.\n\nFirst, concept identification relies on title matching against a legacy lexicon\nthat over-represents the natural sciences and computer science. The\nvocabulary-free replication partially addresses this, but its sample is smaller\nand the verdict is partial.\n\nSecond, the field backbone uses a fixed 26-field classification from OpenAlex.\nA finer-grained classification would produce more adoption episodes but also\nmore noise in field assignment. Our results are conditioned on this specific\nresolution.\n\nThird, the retained-frontier claim is partial by its own pre-registered rule:\nthe volume-matched contrast is null, meaning that we cannot distinguish the\neffect of retention from that of volume. A larger sample with more fine-grained\nvolume controls would be needed to isolate pure retention.\n\nFourth, the openness signal's practical forecasting value is small ($+0.002$\nSpearman on the fresh cohort). The indicators characterise rather than predict:\nthey identify structural preconditions for broad diffusion but do not yield\nindividually actionable forecasts.\n\nFifth, outcomes are measured at $t_0 + 6$ to $t_0 + 8$, a horizon of 6--8\nyears after concept onset. Longer horizons might reveal different dynamics, and\nour results do not speak to very long-term disciplinary integration.\n\nSixth, the analysis is observational. Early network structure is correlated with\nlater breadth, but we cannot establish that it causes broader diffusion. The\nwithin-concept panel analysis suggests that the association is a\nbetween-concept trait rather than a within-concept mechanism.\n\nSeventh, the held-out outcomes were previously unsealed by two earlier\nexperiments in the same project, so the indicator-screen held-out results are\nrobustness checks within the same frame rather than fully independent\nconfirmations. The fresh 2015--2017 cohort is the only body never used in any\nprior step.\n\nEighth, Mathematics and Decision Sciences is underpowered in both the indicator\nscreen (165 concepts) and the retained-frontier model ($d_0 = 0.065$, CI\nincludes zero), so our results may not generalise to this domain.\n\n%% ===================================================================\n\\section{Conclusion}\n\\label{sec:conclusion}\n\nWe have shown that early structural signals in a concept's co-occurrence network\npredict later cross-field breadth across multiple scientific domains, that\nconcepts spread next to fields related to the ones currently retaining them, and\nthat early contact diversity, not continued frontier advance, accounts for most\nof the breadth difference between integrating and localised concepts. The\nopenness signal is topical non-redundancy of the home neighbourhood, not\ntemporal partner turnover. These findings connect the literatures on concept\ndiffusion in science \\citep{Cheng2023}, the principle of relatedness from\neconomic geography \\citep{Hidalgo2007}, and community structure in social\ncontagion \\citep{Weng2013, Ugander2012}, offering a network-level account of\nwhy some scientific concepts become broadly integrated while others remain local.\n\n%% ===================================================================\n\\bibliographystyle{plainnat}\n\\bibliography{references}\n\n\\end{document}\n", "numLines": 651, "startLine": 1, "totalLines": 651}}

# Concepts spread where they stick: network signals of cross-disciplinary diffusion in science

## Overview

This workspace contains a research paper investigating which early structural signals in scientific knowledge networks predict whether a concept will spread broadly across disciplines. The paper identifies seven confirmed network indicators, validates a retained-frontier entry model, and decomposes the breadth gap between integrating and localised concepts.

| File / Directory | Description |

```

Using the full OpenAlex snapshot, we identify thousands of concepts by\ntitle matching, track their adoption episodes across scientific fields, and\nscreen early network indicators against a popularity baseline on held-out field\ngroups never used in selection. Seven indicators survive multiple-testing\ncorrection, and a learned model combining them exceeds the baseline by\n$+0.059$ in Spearman correlation for predicting rarefied cross-field breadth.\nThe retained-frontier hypothesis, that concepts next enter fields related to the\nones currently retaining them, is confirmed in a pre-registered held-out test:\nconditional-logit coefficient $d_0 = 0.322$ [$0.291$, $0.355$], positive in all\nfour domain groups. This extends the principle of\nrelatedness from economic geography to science, with the novel element that\nretention, not merely initial adoption, predicts where a concept goes next.\nA decomposition shows that 73\\% of the breadth gap between integrating and\nlocalised concepts is early contact diversity, while frontier advance\ncontributes near zero. The signal is topical non-redundancy of the early\nneighbourhood, not temporal partner turnover.\n\\end{abstract}\n\n%% ===================================================================\n\\section{Introduction}\n\\label{sec:introduction}\n\nSome scientific concepts stay within their home discipline for decades, while\nothers cross field boundaries within a few years. Optogenetics, originating in\nneuroscience, entered genetics, psychiatry and bioengineering; deep learning,\nrooted in computer science, now appears in medicine, materials science and\nlinguistics. Understanding what distinguishes broadly diffusing concepts from\nlocally absorbed ones matters for science policy, research evaluation and the\ndesign of interdisciplinary programmes \\citep{Cheng2023, Hofstra2019}. If early\nstructural signals predict later cross-field integration, funders and\ninstitutions could identify concepts with high diffusion potential before that\ndiffusion is observable in publication counts alone.\n\nThe problem is hard because simple popularity metrics, including publication\nvolume, growth rate and off-home publication share, already explain much of the\nvariance in later breadth \\citep{Rotolo2015}. Any network indicator must add\ninformation beyond these baselines. Prior work has proposed several candidate\nsignals: community diversity of early adopters \\citep{Weng2013}, collaboration\ndensity before emergence \\citep{Salatino2017}, and structural variation in\ncitation networks \\citep{Salatino2018}. These studies typically operate on\ncurated concept sets without held-out validation, mix concept-level and\nfield-level units of analysis, or do not control for volume-based predictors.\nNo prior study has screened a broad set of temporal knowledge-network indicators\nagainst a shared baseline on held-out field groups for the specific outcome of\nsize-adjusted cross-disciplinary breadth.\n\nA second open question concerns the routes by which concepts move between\nfields. The principle of relatedness, established for regional economic\ndiversification, predicts that actors diversify into activities related to their\nexisting portfolio. For scientific fields adopting new concepts, this principle\nhas been tested for entry but not for the role of currently retaining fields,\nthose that have adopted a concept and kept publishing on it. Whether concepts\nspread next to fields related to the ones currently retaining them, beyond\nrelatedness to the home field alone, is untested.\n\nThis paper addresses both questions with a large-scale empirical study. We\nidentify 12,499 concepts from the OpenAlex bulk snapshot (476 million works),\ncompute 53 early network indicators across seven families, and test them on\nheld-out field groups and a confirmatory onset cohort. We build a\nconditional-logit model of field entry that tests whether retained-field\nrelatedness predicts the next field a concept enters. We decompose the breadth\ngap between integrating and localised concepts into early contact, frontier\nadvance and retention channels.\n\nOur contributions are:\n\\begin{enumerate}\n  \\item We screen 53 early co-occurrence network indicators against a\n    five-feature popularity baseline and confirm seven on held-out field groups\n    for predicting rarefied cross-field breadth, with an ElasticNet combining\n    them exceeding the baseline by $+0.059$ [$+0.046$, $+0.073$] in Spearman\n    correlation.\n  \\item We confirm, in a pre-registered test on 3,162 held-out concepts, that\n    concepts spread next to fields related to the ones currently retaining them\n    (conditional-logit $d_0 = 0.322$ [$0.291$, $0.355$]), extending the principle\n    of relatedness to concept diffusion in science.\n  \\item We decompose the breadth gap between widely and narrowly spreading\n    concepts: 73\\% is early contact diversity, near 0\\% is frontier advance,\n    and 25\\% is differential retention.\n  \\item We show that early neighbourhood consolidation, measured by ideational\n    consistency, predicts volume growth but narrower cross-field reach, a\n    reversal that holds in all five domain groups.\n  \\item We replicate the openness signal on a fresh 2015--2017 cohort (partial\n    Spearman $+0.091$ [$+0.013$, $+0.171$]) and on vocabulary-free newborn\n    phrases.\n\\end{enumerate}\n\nThe remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section~\\ref{sec:related}\nsurveys related work. Section~\\ref{sec:methods} describes the data,\nindicators and models. Section~\\ref{sec:results} presents results.\nSection~\\ref{sec:discussion} discusses the findings, and\nSection~\\ref{sec:limitations} states limitations.\n\n%% ===================================================================\n\\section{Related Work}\n\\label{sec:related}\n\n\\paragraph{Concept diffusion in science.}\n\\citet{Cheng2023} tracked roughly 2,000 new ideas across Web of Science fields\nand found that early social reach, the number of disconnected researcher groups\nadopting an idea, was the strongest predictor of whether an idea became core.\nTheir ideational consistency measure, the cosine similarity of a concept's\nneighbour co-usage vectors across consecutive years, predicted next-year volume.\n\\citet{Rotolo2015} defined emerging technologies through five attributes\nincluding novelty and fast growth but did not test cross-field spread.\n\\citet{Salatino2017} showed that collaboration density rises before topic\nemergence. These studies provide the starting point for our work but do not\nscreen a broad indicator set against a shared baseline with held-out validation\nfor size-adjusted cross-field breadth.\n\n\\paragraph{Topic co-occurrence and citation networks.}\n\\citet{Callon1991} introduced co-word analysis as a tool for mapping the\nstructure of research fields. \\citet{Chavalarias2013} found that dense term\nclusters survive longer, and that density rises during emergence and falls\nbefore decline. \\citet{Salatino2018} proposed the AUGUR system for detecting\ntopic emergence from co-occurrence backbone dynamics. Our work differs in that\nwe test co-occurrence indicators as predictors of a specific outcome, cross-field\nbreadth, rather than using them descriptively.\n\n\\paragraph{Novelty, recombination and impact.}\n\\citet{Uzzi2013} found that high-impact papers combine conventional and atypical\njournal pairings. \\citet{Hofstra2019} documented the diversity--innovation\nparadox: researchers from underrepresented groups produce more novel work but\nreceive fewer citations. \\citet{Tria2013} modelled the dynamics of correlated\nnovelties, showing that novelty begets novelty through the adjacent possible.\n\\citet{Burt2004} showed that structural holes, brokerage positions spanning\ndisconnected groups, generate good ideas. These studies operate at the paper or\nindividual level; ours operates at the concept level and asks about cross-field\nbreadth rather than citation impact.\n\n\\paragraph{The principle of relatedness.}\n\\citet{Hidalgo2007} showed that a country's position in the product space\npredicts which products it diversifies into. \\citet{Neffke2011} extended this to\nregional industry diversification. Our contribution is to test whether\nrelatedness to the set of fields currently retaining a concept predicts entry,\nbeyond relatedness to the home field and conventional density measures.\n\n\\paragraph{Community structure and virality.}\n\\citet{Weng2013} showed that early community diversity predicts virality of\nonline content (AUC $= 0.83$). \\citet{Ugander2012} found that structural\ndiversity drives social contagion on Facebook. \\citet{Centola2010} demonstrated\nexperimentally that complex contagions require reinforcement from multiple\ncommunities. \\citet{Palla2007} tracked the evolution of overlapping communities\nin large networks. Our indicator screen tests the scholarly analogue of these\nmechanisms: whether a concept's early co-occurrence partners spanning multiple\ncommunities predicts later cross-field breadth.\n\n%% ===================================================================\n\\section{Data and Methods}\n\\label{sec:methods}\n\n\\subsection{Concept identification and panel construction}\n\nWe use the OpenAlex bulk snapshot (476,196,327 works; 129.4 million base works\n1995--2022). Concepts are identified by Aho--Corasick title matching of 56,643\nlegacy OpenAlex concepts (levels 2--5) plus Wikidata aliases, with stemmed\nverification. A per-concept precision gate drops concepts with precision below\n0.80 (benchmark precision 0.947, recall 0.659, assessed on a 390-pair benchmark\nwith 60 hand-checked pairs at 90\\% agreement).\n\nA concept's onset year $t_0$ is the first year it reaches 20 grounded\npublications. Home fields are the fields holding at least 40\\% of the first 30\ngrounded papers. The frame comprises 12,499 concepts and 27,393 concept-by-field\nadoption episodes.\n\nThe panel is split by home-field family into a development set (DEV: Computer\nScience, Engineering, Biochemistry/Genetics/Medicine; 4,771 concepts), four\nheld-out field groups (Physical Sciences 742, Life and Environment 1,113, Social\nSciences 1,352, Mathematics and Decision Sciences 165), and a 2010--2014 onset\ncohort (4,356 concepts, all fields). The specification was hash-sealed on DEV\nbefore held-out scoring.\n\n\\subsection{Field backbone}\n\nThe inter-field backbone is a weighted graph over 26 fields, with edge weights\ngiven by positive pointwise mutual information (PMI) of topic co-assignment in a\npre-onset window (1998--2002). This backbone is used throughout for relatedness\ndensity, gateway centrality and community detection. Its time-varying versions\n(computed in five-year slices) correlate at Spearman 0.92 with the frozen version.\n\n\\subsection{Outcome: rarefied cross-field breadth}\n\nThe primary outcome is rarefied cross-field breadth $O_{2r}$ ($m = 50$): the\nexpected number of distinct venue fields among a fixed-size random draw of 50\npapers from a concept's publications in years $t_0 + 6$ to $t_0 + 8$, computed\nby exact hypergeometric rarefaction. Rarefaction separates size-adjusted breadth\nfrom sheer volume. Secondary outcomes include sustained uptake, transience, and\nfield- and year-normalised citation growth.\n\n\\subsection{Baseline}\n\nThe five-feature popularity baseline (B5) is: log publication volume at\n$t_0 + 2$, publication growth rate, log off-home volume, off-home share, and\nnumber of home fields. B5 alone reaches Spearman correlations of 0.65--0.86 with\n$O_{2r}$ across domain groups, setting a high bar for incremental network\nindicators.\n\n\\subsection{Indicator families}\n\nWe compute 53 indicators across seven families in the $t_0$ to $t_0 + 2$\nwindow:\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n  \\item \\textbf{Popularity (E):} publication growth, author growth, author count.\n  \\item \\textbf{Disciplinary composition (F):} Shannon entropy of field\n    distribution, home-field relatedness, Rao--Stirling diversity.\n  \\item \\textbf{Landing position (G):} gateway centrality of home and early\n    off-home fields.\n  \\item \\textbf{Retained-frontier (FR):} relatedness density to fields with\n    revealed comparative advantage (RCA) $> 1$, volume-weighted density, contact\n    reach (count of off-home fields entered), retention ratio (share of contacted\n    fields that retain the concept).\n  \\item \\textbf{Co-occurrence ego-network (A):} 27 indicators from the\n    concept's ego network on the co-occurrence backbone, including neighbourhood\n    novelty (share of new partners), edge persistence (share of retained\n    partners), number of Leiden communities among neighbours, ego density,\n    participation coefficient, brokerage.\n  \\item \\textbf{Co-author ties (S):} author overlap with other concepts.\n  \\item \\textbf{External recognition:} whether the concept appears in domain\n    taxonomies or curated lists.\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\\subsection{Indicator selection and validation}\n\nIndicators are screened on DEV by partial Spearman correlation with $O_{2r}$\ngiven B5, using leave-one-home-group-out cross-validation with 2,000\nconcept-bootstrap resamples. The top-10 frozen indicators per outcome are\nevaluated on held-out groups with DerSimonian--Laird random-effects pooling\nacross four domain groups and Holm correction for multiplicity.\n\n\\subsection{Retained-frontier model}\n\nFor the field-entry analysis, we construct concept-by-target-field-by-year risk\nsets: at each year after onset, every off-home field that the concept has not\nyet entered is at risk. Entry is defined as the concept reaching 5 grounded\npublications in the field. The conditional logit (Breslow partial likelihood) is\nstratified by concept-year, with standardised covariates: relatedness to home,\nlog field size, RCA-based entered-field density, own-field gateway centrality\n(baseline R0); RCA-based density (R1);\nvolume-weighted density (R2); and retained-field relatedness $d_0$ (R3), defined\nas the mean backbone relatedness between the target field and the set of\noff-home fields currently retaining the concept. The specification is frozen on\nDEV and scored once on the held-out frame.\n\n\\subsection{Breadth decomposition}\n\nWe decompose the gap in retained off-home breadth at $t_0 + 8$ between the top\nand bottom $O_{2r}$ terciles into three multiplicative factors: early contact\n$E_2$ (fields entered by $t_0 + 2$), frontier advance $M$ (ratio of fields\nentered by $t_0 + 8$ to those entered by $t_0 + 2$), and retention ratio\n$\\rho$ (share of entered fields retained at $t_0 + 8$). The decomposition is\nvolume-stratified.\n\n%% ===================================================================\n\\section{Results}\n\\label{sec:results}\n\n\\subsection{Which indicators predict cross-field breadth?}\n\nSeven of the 53 screened indicators survive held-out validation with Holm\ncorrection for predicting rarefied cross-field breadth ($O_{2r}$, $m = 50$),\nall positive in six of six domain groups and cohort bodies\n(Table~\\ref{tab:confirmed}).\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Confirmed indicators for rarefied cross-field breadth ($O_{2r}$,\n$m=50$). Pooled partial Spearman correlations from DerSimonian--Laird\nrandom-effects meta-analysis across four held-out domain groups. All seven\nsurvive Holm correction.}\n\\label{tab:confirmed}\n\\begin{tabularx}{\\linewidth}{>{\\raggedright\\arraybackslash}p{4.2cm} c c c c}\n\\toprule\nIndicator & Family & Pooled $\\rho$ & 95\\% CI & $I^2$ \\\\\n\\midrule\nCumulative density of entered fields & FR & $+0.375$ & $[+0.279, +0.462]$ & 0.74 \\\\\nVolume-weighted density & FR & $+0.307$ & $[+0.256, +0.356]$ & 0.10 \\\\\nContact reach (off-home fields entered) & FR & $+0.211$ & $[+0.161, +0.261]$ & 0.00 \\\\\nCommunities among co-occurrence neighbours & A & $+0.167$ & $[+0.063, +0.267]$ & 0.78 \\\\\nNeighbourhood novelty & A & $+0.151$ & $[+0.044, +0.255]$ & 0.75 \\\\\nRetention ratio of contacted fields & FR & $-0.114$ & $[-0.160, -0.067]$ & 0.00 \\\\\nEgo-network density & A & $-0.102$ & $[-0.151, -0.053]$ & 0.00 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabularx}\n\\end{table}\n\nThe first two indicators, cumulative density and volume-weighted density, use\nthe cumulative field history up to $t_0 + 2$ and partly reflect a pre-onset\nfootprint. After removing the pre-onset component, the post-onset\nvolume-weighted density attenuates to about half its raw value ($+0.176$ vs\n$+0.307$) and is nearly rank-identical to the B5 reach baseline (Spearman\nbetween the two $> 0.97$). The remaining indicators, contact reach, community\ncount, novelty, retention ratio and ego density, measure genuinely early\nstructural properties.\n\nA learned ElasticNet combining the confirmed indicators exceeds B5 by $+0.059$\n[$+0.046$, $+0.073$] in Spearman correlation on the pooled held-out set.\nPer-group held-out increments are: Physical Sciences $+0.050$, Life and\nEnvironment $+0.059$, Social Sciences $+0.062$, Mathematics and Decision\nSciences $+0.037$.\n\nFor sustained uptake, only the number of early authors is confirmed. For\ncitation growth, home-field relatedness (negative) and author growth are\nconfirmed but the learned model reaches only Spearman 0.188 against B5's 0.015.\nExternal recognition shows no association with any network indicator beyond\nonset year.\n\n\\subsection{Openness composite and confirmation}\n\nThe six ego-network components of the confirmed indicators compose into an\nopenness index (OPEN), defined as the mean of six $z$-scored components with\nconstants frozen on the full 12,499-concept frame.\n\nOn a fresh 2015--2017 onset cohort of 1,443 concepts never used in any selection\nstep, OPEN measured within the home field (OPEN\\textsubscript{home}) shows a\npartial Spearman correlation with $O_{2r}$ of $+0.091$ [$+0.013$, $+0.171$] at\nthe second control rung (controlling for B5, onset year and contact reach), and\n$+0.080$ [$+0.001$, $+0.162$] at the third rung (adding concept type and\npre-onset footprint). The confidence interval includes zero at higher rungs, and\nthe DerSimonian--Laird pool across groups is $+0.083$ [$-0.007$, $+0.173$]. The\nsignal carries no forecasting gain over B5 ($+0.002$ Spearman). The\npre-registered verdict is confirmed but marginal.\n\nAn evidence synthesis across six non-selection bodies (four held-out domain\ngroups plus the 2010--2014 and 2015--2017 cohorts) gives a DerSimonian--Laird\npooled OPEN\\textsubscript{home} partial Spearman of $+0.069$ [$+0.038$,\n$+0.100$] with $I^2 = 0$, all six bodies positive. The selection-body (DEV)\nestimate of $+0.109$ shows shrinkage of $1.58\\times$ relative to the\nnon-selection pool.\n\nNeighbourhood novelty carries the openness signal. The pooled partial Spearman\nof neighbourhood novelty and churn across five non-selection bodies is $+0.105$\n[$+0.069$, $+0.140$] with $I^2 = 0$, while edge persistence is null on the\nfresh cohort. Figure~\\ref{fig:evidence_synthesis} summarises the evidence\nacross all evaluation bodies.\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig2_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Partial Spearman correlation between home-field openness (OPEN\\_home) and rarefied cross-field breadth ($O_{2r}$, $m=50$), controlling for the five-feature popularity baseline B5 (rung R2), per evaluation body. Blue squares are the six non-selection bodies: four held-out domain groups and the 2010--14 and 2015--17 onset cohorts. Square area is proportional to inverse-variance (Fisher-$z$) weight, and horizontal lines are 95\\% bootstrap CIs (2,000 concept resamples); $n$ is the number of concepts analysed. The blue diamond spans the DerSimonian--Laird random-effects pool over these six bodies, $+0.069$ [$+0.038$, $+0.100$] with $I^2=0$, and the dotted blue line marks the pooled estimate. The grey row is the DEV selection body ($+0.109$ [$+0.073$, $+0.144$], $n=3{,}003$), on which the index was chosen. It is not part of the pool and is $1.58\\times$ the pooled estimate, consistent with winner's-curse shrinkage. The dashed grey line marks zero. All six non-selection estimates are positive, but only the two cohort intervals exclude zero. Because five of the six bodies had been unsealed earlier, the pool is descriptive rather than confirmatory.}\n  \\label{fig:evidence_synthesis}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsection{Confound analysis: topical dispersion, not temporal churn}\n\nThe openness signal could be an artefact of small yearly samples. We test this\nwith four null models:\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n  \\item \\textbf{Fixed-$n$ rarefaction} (V1, drawing $n = 10$ partners per year):\n    neighbourhood novelty and churn retains 68\\% of the raw effect (pooled\n    $+0.078$ vs $+0.116$).\n  \\item \\textbf{Within-concept year-permutation} (V2, 200 permutations): the\n    temporal excess is $+0.008$ with split-half reliability below 0.05,\n    indicating that the time-ordering of partner arrivals contributes almost\n    nothing.\n  \\item \\textbf{Configuration-model null} (V3, degree-preserving rewiring): ego\n    density normalised against the null ($z$-scored) still predicts breadth\n    (partial Spearman $-0.091$).\n  \\item \\textbf{Split-half reliability} (V4): neighbourhood novelty and churn\n    raw $= 0.48$, OPEN\\textsubscript{home} $= 0.49$, rising to 0.58 after\n    configuration-null cleaning.\n\\end{itemize}\n\nRaw edge persistence is 66\\% explained by its own within-concept permutation\nnull mean, and that null mean predicts the outcome at least as strongly as raw\npersistence itself. The signal is a static topical-dispersion property of the\nhome topic mix, not temporal partner turnover.\n\n\\subsection{Reconciling consistency and breadth}\n\n\\citet{Cheng2023} reported that ideational consistency (cosine of a concept's\ntopic co-usage vector across consecutive years) predicts next-year volume with\na 53\\% increase per standard deviation. We reproduce this almost exactly: our\ntwin negative-binomial model gives $+53.5\\%$ per SD. Adding log current volume\nreduces this to $+1.3\\%$ [$+0.5\\%$, $+2.1\\%$]: the raw association is\nsize-dominated.\n\nNet of size, consistency's partial Spearman with rarefied cross-field breadth is\n$-0.069$ [$-0.093$, $-0.047$], negative in all five domain groups. On the\n2015--2017 cohort, the reversal replicates at $-0.111$ [$-0.197$, $-0.030$].\nWithin-concept panel analysis shows that years of high consistency are followed\nby slightly more off-home entries ($b = +0.025$ [$+0.004$, $+0.048$]), so the\nreach penalty is a between-concept trait, not a within-concept mechanism.\n\nConsistency and breadth are not opposed at the within-concept level, but\nconcepts whose neighbourhood is consistently structured tend to grow in volume\nrather than spreading across fields. This complements \\citet{Cheng2023} by\nseparating the volume and breadth outcomes.\n\n\\subsection{How do concepts diffuse across fields?}\n\n\\subsubsection{Retained-frontier entry}\n\nThe conditional-logit model tests whether a concept's next field of entry is\npredicted by the target field's relatedness to the off-home fields that\ncurrently retain the concept, beyond relatedness to the home field, field size,\nentered-field density and own gateway centrality.\n\nOn the development frame (274 concepts, 961 informative strata), the model\nreproduces a prior result: likelihood-ratio 68.6, $d_0 = 0.281$.\n\nOn the independent held-out frame (3,162 concepts, 6,978 entry events,\nhash-frozen specification), the retained-frontier coefficient is $d_0 = 0.322$\n[$0.291$, $0.355$] with concept-clustered standard errors (R3 vs R2\nlikelihood-ratio 325.8, $p < 10^{-72}$). The result is positive in all four\nheld-out domain groups: Physical Sciences 0.148, Life and Environment 0.401,\nSocial Sciences 0.297, Mathematics and Decision Sciences 0.065\n(underpowered). The DerSimonian--Laird pool over four groups gives 0.243\n[$0.118$, $0.368$] with $I^2 = 0.92$, reflecting genuine heterogeneity across\ndomains. Retained-label permutation $p = 0.001$; backbone-rewiring permutation\n$p = 0.004$; node-label permutation $p = 0.003$.\n\nThe pre-declared volume-matched contrast, comparing entry rates of retained\nversus entered-but-not-retained fields in the same volume cell, is null:\n$-0.028$ [$-0.105$, $+0.046$]. The frozen verdict is therefore partial:\npersistence is confounded with volume. Under a minimum-conditional-probability\nproximity \\citep{Hidalgo2007}, the retained-frontier coefficient reverses to\n$-0.021$ ($p = 0.012$), indicating backbone dependence.\nTable~\\ref{tab:retained_frontier} reports all domain-group estimates.\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Retained-frontier coefficient $d_0$ from the conditional-logit model\nof next-field entry across domain groups and the 2010--2014 cohort, with 95\\%\nconcept-clustered confidence intervals.}\n\\label{tab:retained_frontier}\n\\begin{tabular}{l c c c}\n\\toprule\nModel & $d_0$ coefficient & 95\\% CI (concept) & Likelihood ratio \\\\\n\\midrule\nDevelopment set & 0.228 & $[0.164, 0.291]$ & 34.5 \\\\\nHeld-out pooled & 0.322 & $[0.291, 0.355]$ & 325.8 \\\\\nPhysical Sciences & 0.148 & $[0.078, 0.219]$ & -- \\\\\nLife \\& Environment & 0.401 & $[0.342, 0.460]$ & -- \\\\\nSocial Sciences & 0.297 & $[0.246, 0.348]$ & -- \\\\\nMath \\& Decision Sci. & 0.065 & $[-0.109, 0.239]$ & -- \\\\\n2010--2014 cohort & 0.321 & $[0.292, 0.347]$ & -- \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig3_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Retained-frontier coefficient $d_0$ from the conditional-logit model of next-field entry, estimated on held-out data. $d_0$ measures how much a target field's relatedness to the fields currently retaining a concept predicts entry into it. It is net of relatedness to the home field, field size, entered-field density and gateway centrality, and is expressed in log-odds per standard deviation. Blue circles are the estimates for the four held-out domain groups (top) and for the 2010--14 held-out cohort. Horizontal bars are 95\\% Wald confidence intervals from concept-clustered standard errors, and $n$ is the number of entry events. The dark diamond spans the DerSimonian--Laird random-effects pooled estimate over the four groups, 0.243 [0.118, 0.368], with $I^2 = 0.92$. The dashed vertical line marks $d_0 = 0$, and the right-hand column prints each estimate with its interval. The point estimate is positive in all four groups and in the cohort. The interval excludes zero for Physical Sciences, Life \\& Env., Social Sciences and the cohort. Math \\& Decision ($n = 296$) is the weak, imprecise group, 0.065 [$-0.109$, 0.239], and together with Life \\& Env.\\ (0.401) it drives the high heterogeneity. These are associations. In the same experiment, a volume-matched contrast between retaining and non-retaining fields is null ($-0.028$ [$-0.105$, 0.046]; not plotted), so the pre-registered frontier test is only partially supported: persistence is confounded with volume.}\n  \\label{fig:retained_frontier}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig4_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Nested conditional-logit models of field entry on the held-out frame (3,162 concepts, 6,978 entry events, 6,076 informative concept-year strata). R0: home relatedness + log field size + entered-field density + own-field gateway centrality; R1: + RCA-based density; R2: + volume-weighted density; R3: + retained-frontier relatedness. (a)~Within-stratum AUC of each rung. Blue circles, solid line: primary specification using backbone relatedness. Amber squares, dashed line: sensitivity rebuild using minimum conditional-probability proximity. (b)~Likelihood-ratio $\\chi^2$ (df $=1$, log scale) for the term each rung adds over the previous rung. Solid blue bars: primary. Hatched amber bars: sensitivity. The dotted line marks $p=0.05$ ($\\chi^2=3.84$). In the primary specification, the retained-frontier term gives the largest step (LR $=325.8$, $p<10^{-72}$), but AUC rises only from 0.847 to 0.852. The volume-density step is not significant (LR $=1.9$). Under minimum conditional-probability proximity, baseline discrimination is higher and the retained-frontier term adds no AUC (0.867 to 0.866; LR $=6.3$). The increment therefore depends on the proximity definition. No confidence intervals on AUC are available.}\n  \\label{fig:model_ladder}\n\\end{figure}\n\nFigure~\\ref{fig:retained_frontier} shows the per-group estimates, and\nFigure~\\ref{fig:model_ladder} displays the nested model ladder. The\nwithin-stratum AUC increases from 0.847 (R2: baseline + RCA density + volume\ndensity) to 0.852 (R3: + retained-frontier relatedness). The increment is small\nbecause field size alone achieves AUC 0.76, density only 0.59, and the ceiling\nis constrained by having only 26 fields.\n\n\\subsubsection{Gateway centrality does not predict retention}\n\nA separate pre-registered test asks whether the adopting field's eigenvector\ncentrality on the backbone predicts retention. On 27,393 held-out episodes, the\ngateway-centrality increment is effectively zero: $\\Delta$-AUC $-0.00001$\n[$-0.0006$, $+0.0003$]. The minimum detectable effect is 0.004. Gateway alone\nhas AUC 0.605 on DEV versus 0.506 on held-out: the DEV signal is\ndomain-specific. Verdict: disconfirmed.\n\n\\subsubsection{Breadth decomposition}\n\nWe decompose the gap in retained off-home breadth between the top and bottom\n$O_{2r}$ terciles into log $E_2$ (early contact), log $M$ (frontier advance)\nand log $\\rho$ (retention). Volume-stratified, on the held-out pool excluding\nMedicine (to avoid a domain that dominates the localised class):\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n  \\item Early contact share: 73.3\\%\n  \\item Frontier advance share: 1.3\\%\n  \\item Retention share: 25.4\\%\n  \\item Difference (exploration minus retention): 0.492 [$0.403$, $0.575$]\n\\end{itemize}\n\nThe DerSimonian--Laird pool of the exploration-retention difference across three\nheld-out groups is 0.504 [$0.329$, $0.679$] with $I^2 = 0.76$.\n\nBreadth differences between concepts are set by how many fields a concept\ncontacts early, not by how many more it enters later. Frontier advance, the\nratio of fields at $t_0 + 8$ to those at $t_0 + 2$, contributes near zero\nbecause both broad and narrow concepts gain new fields at similar rates relative\nto their base (Figure~\\ref{fig:decomposition}).\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig5_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Decomposition of the gap in retained off-home breadth (log scale) between the top and bottom $O_{2r}$ tercile into three multiplicative channels: early contact ($E_2$, green), frontier advance ($M$, light grey) and retention ($\\rho$, blue). The left bar stacks the three shares into the total gap (share $=1$; total log gap $D_{\\text{total}}=1.035$, 95\\% CI $[0.957, 1.108]$). The other three bars show each channel's share of the gap with 95\\% percentile confidence intervals from 2{,}000 concept bootstraps, with terciles and volume quintiles recomputed in each resample. The sample is the held-out pool (PHYS, LIFEENV, SOC, MATHDEC), volume-stratified, excluding Medicine homes ($n=1{,}825$ concepts). Early contact accounts for 73\\% of the gap (0.733, $[0.688, 0.789]$), retention for 25\\% (0.254, $[0.213, 0.298]$), and frontier advance for close to zero (0.013, $[-0.027, 0.047]$). The shares are an accounting identity for the breadth outcome, not causal effects.}\n  \\label{fig:decomposition}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsubsection{Diffusion trajectories: a continuum, not types}\n\nWe tested whether concepts cluster into discrete trajectory types (localised\nemergence, rapid interdisciplinary diffusion, gradual integration) using DTW\n$k$-medoids and HMM-based clustering on state sequences of field presence. No\ntrajectory typology passes a naming rule: the adjusted Rand index between DTW\n$k = 4$ and HMM $S = 5$ is 0.222, and held-out re-clustering gives ARI $= 0.44$.\nInstead, PCA reveals a continuum: PC1 (38.8\\% of variance) is a\nbreadth-of-spread axis, and PC2 (10.7\\%) is a keep-versus-lose axis. Early\nopenness (OPEN) correlates with PC1 beyond B5 (held-out DerSimonian--Laird\npartial correlation 0.120, $I^2 = 0$) but not with PC2.\n\n\\subsection{Replication on vocabulary-free concepts}\n\nTo test whether the openness signal depends on the legacy concept lexicon, we\nconstructed a separate frame of 636 newborn title noun phrases (onsets\n2003--2015) absent from the 56,643 legacy concepts. On this frame,\nOPEN\\textsubscript{home} shows a partial Spearman with rarefied breadth\n($O_{2r}$, $m = 30$) of $+0.117$ [$+0.020$, $+0.218$] at the third control\nrung, and neighbourhood novelty and churn of $+0.108$ [$+0.007$, $+0.211$].\nThree of four estimable domain groups are positive. The verdict is partial: the\nconfidence interval on OPEN\\textsubscript{home} includes zero at R5, and the\nHolm-corrected $p$-value is 0.052.\n\n%% ===================================================================\n\\section{Discussion}\n\\label{sec:discussion}\n\nOur results address both research questions posed in the Introduction.\n\nFor RQ1, seven temporal network indicators predict cross-field breadth beyond a\nstrong popularity baseline, and these indicators generalise across four held-out\nscientific domain groups. The strongest are contact reach (the count of off-home\nfields already entered) and neighbourhood novelty (the share of new\nco-occurrence partners). A learned model improves Spearman correlation by\n$+0.059$ over the baseline. The practical forecasting gain is modest: B5 already\nexplains most of the variance, and OPEN adds only $+0.002$ Spearman on the\nfresh cohort. The signal identifies which concepts are structurally positioned\nfor broader diffusion, rather than providing strong individual-level forecasts.\n\nThe confound analysis reveals that the signal is topical non-redundancy, a\nstatic structural property of the home topic mix, rather than temporal partner\nturnover.
